# Lock and load

Twenty minutes, once, in hour one. It creates the scaffolding that makes every later
session disciplined: the rules file, the continuity files, the git hygiene, and a commit
plan.

Run it after the idea is chosen and before the first feature. It does **not** replace
`/skillz:architecture`, which designs the system. This sets up the repo the system will
live in, and the two run back to back in hour one.

**Read `CONFIG.md` before anything else.**

**Per-event config lives in the project, not here.** If the hackathon repo has a
`hackathon.yml` at its root, read that first; the values below are defaults. At the
start of an event, copy this skill's `CONFIG.md` into a `hackathon.yml` at the project
root and edit that copy, so a plugin update never overwrites your settings.

## The rule that governs everything

> Set up the repo for the history judges will read, not just for the code you are about
> to write.

Organizers check commit history to confirm the work happened during the event. That
makes your history a judged artifact, not a byproduct. A log showing steady progress
across the weekend reads as engineering; four giant commits read as a dump, or worse, as
code that existed before the event.

## Time budget

| # | Phase | Wall clock | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Inspect what is already here | 3 min | New, existing or partial, and what to preserve |
| 2 | Git hygiene | 5 min | `.gitignore`, no secrets, first commit |
| 3 | The three files | 7 min | `CLAUDE.md`, `handoff.md`, `memory.md` |
| 4 | Commit roadmap | 5 min | Natural commit boundaries from the build order |

**This must not delay the deploy.** `/skillz:architecture` wants a URL to exist in hour
one, and that outranks this. Run them in parallel: one person deploys an empty app while
another runs this, or run this immediately after the deploy lands.

```bash
bash assets/init.sh          # does phases 2 and 3 in about thirty seconds
```

## Step 1 - Inspect first

Never overwrite instructions you have not read.

```bash
ls -a; cat README.md CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md 2>/dev/null | head -40
cat package.json 2>/dev/null | head -30
git log --oneline | head -10; git status --short
cat .gitignore 2>/dev/null
```

Classify what you have, because the answer changes everything after it:

| State | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Empty directory** | Full setup. Nothing to preserve |
| **Fresh scaffold** (create-next-app and nothing else) | Full setup. Keep the generated `.gitignore` and add to it |
| **Existing project** | Read every instruction file before touching it. Add, do not replace |
| **Pre-existing code being adapted** | **Check the rules.** Many events restrict pre-existing code, and commits predating the window are a disqualification risk. Resolve this before writing anything |

That last row is the one that ends hackathons, and it is a five minute check.

## Step 2 - Git hygiene

### What never gets committed

```text
.env, .env.local, .env*.local      secrets
node_modules/, .next/, dist/        regenerable
*.log, .DS_Store                    noise
any private key, on any network     see the house rules
```

Verify rather than assume, because a key in history stays in history:

```bash
git ls-files | grep -E "^\.env$|^\.env\.local$" && echo "REMOVE AND ROTATE"
git log --all -p 2>/dev/null | grep -icE "sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{20}|PRIVATE_KEY=[^[:space:]]"
```

Commit `.env.example` with every key present and every value empty.

### What does get committed, despite the temptation

**Do not blanket-ignore markdown.** The rule `*.md` with `!README.md` looks tidy and
quietly breaks two other skills:

- `/skillz:readme` and `/skillz:polish` create `docs/architecture.md`,
  `docs/integrations.md`, `docs/evaluation-map.md` and `docs/technical-decisions.md`.
  Those are judge-facing evidence. A sponsor judge clicks them. Ignored, they do not
  exist.
- `handoff.md` ignored means a teammate who was asleep cannot read it. The whole point
  of a handoff is that someone else resumes from it, so a local-only handoff works for
  one person on one machine and fails everywhere else.

The real goal behind the instinct is a repo root that looks intentional. Get that by
putting the operational files somewhere deliberate, not by hiding them:

| Layout | Root contains | Choose when |
|---|---|---|
| **Flat** (default) | `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `handoff.md`, `memory.md` | Solo or pair. Simplest |
| **`.hack/`** | `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` only | Three or more people, or you want the tidiest tree |

Both commit everything. Set `repo.layout` in CONFIG. Full reasoning and the drop-in
file: `references/repo-hygiene.md` and `assets/gitignore`.

## Step 3 - The three files

| File | Job | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `CLAUDE.md` | The working stance, read every session | `../workflow/assets/CLAUDE.md` |
| `handoff.md` | Where work stopped, and the next step | `../workflow/assets/handoff.md` |
| `memory.md` | Durable project knowledge | `../workflow/assets/memory.md` |

Copy them, then fill in the project specifics: the commands, the demo path files, the
deployed URL. An unfilled `CLAUDE.md` is worse than none, because it costs context every
session and says nothing.

`/skillz:workflow` owns how these are maintained during the build. This skill only
creates them. Do not duplicate its guidance here.

The one rule worth repeating at init, because it is the one that decays: **`handoff.md`
gets updated at every checkpoint, not at session end.** You will not know which
checkpoint was the last one.

## Step 4 - The commit roadmap

Do not invent a second plan. Take the build order from
`../architecture/references/build-order.md` and mark the commit boundaries on it.

```text
Phase            Commits   Boundary
Foundation       1-6       scaffold, deploy, tokens, shell, types, seed
Walking skeleton 7-12      one request end to end, API, schema, render
The aha path     13-24     the hard part, in working increments
Rest of demo     25-34     remaining screens and routes
States + errors  35-42     empty, loading, error, partial, success, fallbacks
Hardening        43-50     demo-proofing, README, fixtures, recording
```

That is a planning tool, not a quota. Numbers are illustrative; the real boundaries come
from your build order.

### The target, and the actual reason for it

**Aim for 50 or more meaningful commits.** Over a 36 hour event that is roughly one
every 45 minutes, which is a natural working rhythm rather than a stretch.

The reason is not neatness. Organizers check history to confirm the work happened in the
window, and a judge who opens your commits sees one of two stories:

```text
52 commits, steady across two days, readable messages   a team that built something
4 commits, three of them in the last hour               a dump, or pre-existing code
```

**Never manufacture commits to hit the number.** `fix`, `update`, `changes`, `final`,
`final2` are worse than a smaller honest count, because they are visibly padding and
padding reads as insecurity. A real 30 beats a fake 50.

Message format, the anti-spam rules, and what a strong history looks like:
`references/commit-history.md`.

## Commit discipline

Every commit is one coherent unit that leaves the project working.

```text
feat: add wallet connection flow
fix: handle expired session tokens
test: cover settlement retry behavior
refactor: simplify transaction service
docs: document sponsor integration
chore: configure deployment environment
```

Three hard rules, all from the house rules and all checkable:

- **No em dashes** in commit messages.
- **No AI attribution.** No `Co-Authored-By` naming a tool, no generated-by footer, no
  robot emoji. History is a surface judges read.
- **No secrets.** Ever, on any network.

Before each commit:

```text
[ ] One purpose, and the project still runs
[ ] Only related changes
[ ] I actually verified the behavior I am claiming
[ ] Message is specific, no em dash, no AI trailer
[ ] handoff.md reflects reality
```

## Honest test records

Record what you ran, in `handoff.md`, with real numbers:

```text
Ran:    npm test -- settlement
Result: 12 passed, 0 failed
Covers: payout path and the cap rejection
```

**Never claim a test you did not run, and never invent a count.** An unticked box is
useful information; a ticked box nobody exercised removes the next person's reason to
look. `../workflow/references/verification.md` has the escalation ladder.

## What not to do at init

- **Do not build features.** This is twenty minutes of setup, then you build.
- **Do not pre-create empty commits** to seed the count.
- **Do not add CI, Docker, husky or a monorepo tool.** None of them score, all of them
  cost an hour, and a pre-commit hook that fails at 3am is a real risk.
- **Do not write a test suite.** One smoke test of the demo path, later.
- **Do not rewrite an existing project's conventions** to match your preferences.
- **Do not delay the deploy.** A URL in hour one outranks everything here.

## Time traps

- **Perfecting `CLAUDE.md`.** Fill the commands and the demo path. Refine it later or never.
- **Designing a branch strategy** before anyone has pushed. Default to `main`, add
  branches when two people actually collide.
- **A commit roadmap with forty line items.** Six phases is enough to work from.
- **Running this twice.** It is an init skill. After the first run, `/skillz:workflow`
  owns the ongoing discipline.

## Report

```text
LOCKED AND LOADED

Created      CLAUDE.md, handoff.md, memory.md, .gitignore, .env.example
Preserved    [anything that already existed and was kept]
Layout       flat | .hack/
Commits      1 (initial). Roadmap: 6 phases, ~50 boundaries
Verified     no secrets tracked, no secrets in history, build green

State        [one line on where the project actually is]
Next         [the exact next task, with the file]
```

## Handoff

`/skillz:architecture` next, if it has not already run in parallel. Then
`/skillz:workflow` governs every session from here, and `version-control` for the git
problems that arrive later: a four-way merge at 3am, and recovery from the one that ate
the demo.

# Lock and load customization

Defaults. Copy into `hackathon.yml` at your project root and edit there.

```yaml
# ── Repo layout ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
repo:
  layout:          flat        # flat | .hack/. see references/repo-hygiene.md
                               # flat: handoff.md, memory.md at root
                               # .hack/: both in a .hack/ folder, root stays tidy
  commit_ops_files: true       # handoff and memory are SHARED. never gitignore them
  ignore_markdown: false       # never blanket-ignore *.md. docs/ is judge evidence

# ── State on arrival ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
project:
  state:           auto        # empty | scaffold | existing | pre-existing-code
  event_window:    auto        # start date. commits before it are a rules question

# ── Commits ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
commits:
  target:          50          # a direction, not a quota. real 30 beats fake 50
  format:          conventional # feat | fix | test | refactor | docs | chore | perf
  em_dashes:       forbidden
  ai_attribution:  forbidden   # not configurable
  roadmap_phases:  6

# ── Init scope ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
init:
  cap_min:         20
  ci:              none        # none. a failing hook at 3am is a real risk
  hooks:           none
  blocks_deploy:   false       # the deploy in hour one outranks this skill
```

## How the knobs bite

| Knob | Effect |
|---|---|
| `repo.layout: .hack/` | `handoff.md` and `memory.md` go in `.hack/`. `CLAUDE.md` stays at root because Claude Code reads it from there. Update `/skillz:workflow`'s `continuity.*` paths to match |
| `repo.commit_ops_files: false` | Only safe for a solo dev on one machine. Breaks every handoff to another person |
| `repo.ignore_markdown: true` | Refused unless `docs/` is explicitly re-included, because it hides judge-facing evidence |
| `project.state: pre-existing-code` | Stops and checks the event's rules on prior work before anything else |
| `commits.target` | Shapes the roadmap granularity. Never justifies a padding commit |
| `init.ci` / `init.hooks` | Left off. Neither scores and both can fail at the worst moment |

## The one that is usually wrong

`repo.ignore_markdown`. It is set to true because a root full of markdown files looks
messy and the obvious fix is to hide them. The problem is that the files it hides are
exactly the ones other people need: the docs a sponsor judge clicks, and the handoff a
teammate wakes up to. Use `layout: .hack/` instead. It gets the tidy root without hiding
anything.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# init.sh - lock and load a hackathon repo in about thirty seconds.
#
# Run from the root of the HACKATHON project (not the skill library):
#   bash <path-to-skill>/assets/init.sh            # flat layout
#   bash <path-to-skill>/assets/init.sh --hack     # .hack/ layout
#
# Safe to run on an existing project: it never overwrites a file that
# already exists, it appends to .gitignore instead of replacing it, and it
# reports everything it skipped.
#
# It does NOT make a commit. Review what it created, then commit yourself.

set -uo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
WORKFLOW="$HERE/../../workflow/assets"
LAYOUT="flat"
[ "${1:-}" = "--hack" ] && LAYOUT="hack"

grn() { printf '\033[32m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
ylw() { printf '\033[33m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
red() { printf '\033[31m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }

CREATED=(); SKIPPED=()

place() { # place <src> <dest>
  if [ -e "$2" ]; then SKIPPED+=("$2 (exists, kept)"); return; fi
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$2")"
  cp "$1" "$2" && CREATED+=("$2")
}

# ── 0. Sanity ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [ ! -d "$WORKFLOW" ]; then
  red "cannot find the workflow skill's assets at $WORKFLOW"
  red "run this from inside the installed skillz plugin, or adjust WORKFLOW"
  exit 1
fi

# ── 1. Git ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if ! git rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  git init -q . && CREATED+=(".git")
fi

# ── 2. .gitignore: append, never replace ───────────────────────────────────
if [ -f .gitignore ]; then
  if grep -q "Deliberately NOT ignored" .gitignore; then
    SKIPPED+=(".gitignore (already has the lock-and-load block)")
  else
    { echo ""; echo "# ── lock-and-load ──"; cat "$HERE/gitignore"; } >> .gitignore
    CREATED+=(".gitignore (appended)")
  fi
else
  cp "$HERE/gitignore" .gitignore && CREATED+=(".gitignore")
fi

# Warn about the markdown trap if someone already set it
if grep -qE '^\*\.md$' .gitignore 2>/dev/null; then
  red "WARNING: .gitignore ignores *.md. That hides docs/ (judge evidence) and"
  red "         handoff.md (shared continuity). See references/repo-hygiene.md"
fi

# ── 3. .env.example ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [ ! -e .env.example ]; then
  printf '# Every key the app reads, with an empty value and where to get one.\n' > .env.example
  if [ -d src ]; then
    grep -rhoE 'process\.env\.[A-Z_0-9]+' src/ 2>/dev/null \
      | sed 's/process\.env\.//' | sort -u | sed 's/$/=/' >> .env.example
  fi
  CREATED+=(".env.example")
fi

# ── 4. The three files ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
place "$WORKFLOW/CLAUDE.md" "CLAUDE.md"
if [ "$LAYOUT" = "hack" ]; then
  place "$WORKFLOW/handoff.md" ".hack/handoff.md"
  place "$WORKFLOW/memory.md"  ".hack/memory.md"
else
  place "$WORKFLOW/handoff.md" "handoff.md"
  place "$WORKFLOW/memory.md"  "memory.md"
fi

# ── 5. Secrets check ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LEAK=0
git ls-files 2>/dev/null | grep -qE '^\.env(\.local)?$' && { red "TRACKED .env file: git rm --cached it and ROTATE the keys"; LEAK=1; }
if git log -1 >/dev/null 2>&1 && git log --all -p 2>/dev/null | grep -qE 'sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{20}|PRIVATE_KEY=[^[:space:]]'; then
  red "A SECRET IS IN GIT HISTORY. Rotate it. Rewriting history is not enough."; LEAK=1
fi

# ── 6. Pre-existing work ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
if git log -1 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  FIRST=$(git log --reverse --format='%ad' --date=short | head -1)
  ylw "first commit: $FIRST. if that predates the event, check the rules on prior work"
fi

# ── Report ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo
grn "LOCKED AND LOADED  (layout: $LAYOUT)"
for f in "${CREATED[@]}"; do echo "  created   $f"; done
for f in "${SKIPPED[@]}"; do echo "  kept      $f"; done
[ $LEAK -eq 0 ] && grn "  no secrets tracked or in history"
echo
ylw "next:"
echo "  1. fill in CLAUDE.md: the commands, the demo path files, the deployed URL"
echo "  2. note where to get each key in .env.example"
echo "  3. review, then commit:  git add -A && git commit -m \"chore: initialize project workflow\""
[ "$LAYOUT" = "hack" ] && echo "  4. set /skillz:workflow continuity paths to .hack/ in hackathon.yml"
exit 0

# Revenant

> **It catches coding agents that made the tests pass by editing the tests, and reverts them.**

We built **Revenant** for **teams that let coding agents commit**, letting them **find and undo the commits that only passed because the agent changed the exam**, using **Entire checkpoints and replays pinned to each commit's parent** to make **auditing an agent's past decisions** possible.

Built for neatHack (October 10 to 12, 2026). One track: an agent, or a team of agents, that finishes a substantial task from start to finish. Required tools: neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai.

The product rule, in the README and in the demo:

> Revenant never proposes a new feature. It only keeps, reverts, or marks a decision stale or frozen. If it cannot prove the original decision wrong, it does not guess. A missing checkpoint freezes the item, and Revenant never reverts a line a human wrote.

## Why this and not another fixer

Most hackathon agents ship a fix. Revenant's finished task is a signed ledger: these commits should be reverted, these stay, this one expired because the code it relies on changed, this one cannot be retried. The unit of work is a past agent action, not an open issue.

CI cannot do this, for two reasons. CI runs the tests in the commit, which are the tests the agent may have edited. And CI does not know what the agent was asked to do. Revenant runs the tests as they were before the agent touched them, and reads the prompt from the Entire checkpoint to decide whether a test change was allowed. It also works on history you have already merged.

## The hero case: the agent graded its own exam

Run on 2026-10-09 with Entire CLI 0.11.4 and jest. A commit broke the discount math and changed the test's expected value to match:

```text
Commit's own tests vs parent baseline:
  VERDICT: PASS ... Verification is complete; no further test runs are needed.
Parent's tests run against the commit's code:
  NEWLY FAILING (1): ./charge.test.js > ten percent off
  VERDICT: REGRESSION in 1 test: ./charge.test.js > ten percent off
```

Those two results side by side are the first 45 seconds of the demo.

The checkpoint decides what the result means, because **the prompt is the warrant**. "Fix the rounding bug" does not authorize changing what 10% off equals. "VIP discounts are now doubled, update the tests" does. With no checkpoint, nobody can tell, so the item freezes.

Pitch this as building on `entire graph verify`, not beating it. `verify` answers "did this change break the tests as they are now?" It cannot know the tests themselves were edited. Revenant adds that question. Entire's team is on the judging panel.

The same replay catches every way of editing the exam: a changed expected value, an added skip, a deleted test, or test config that filters a test out. In each case the parent's version runs and fails.

## The trial

### What is on trial

A triple: `(commit, checkpoint, trace)`.

- **Commit:** its trailer `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` names the checkpoint. Since Entire 0.10.0 the ID is a 26-character ULID such as `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`, stored under `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`. Older repos use 12-character hex IDs on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Parse both.
- **Checkpoint:** one or more sessions, each with prompts, transcript, tool calls and tokens. One session can produce several commits, so read only the turns before this commit. Commands: `entire checkpoint explain <sha> --json` for metadata, and `--transcript --session-index N` for each session's JSONL.
- **Trace:** the neatlogs Claude Code plugin copies Claude Code's session ID into the `neatlogs.session.id` attribute of every span. Fetch it with `neatlogs traces list --session <id>` and `neatlogs traces raw-spans <trace-id>`. This join is the first thing to confirm with a real key.

Attribution is per commit. Entire counts agent lines and human lines for each commit and has no line ranges, so Revenant never tries to split a hunk. A revert that would touch a mixed commit becomes a freeze.

### When a past action is wrong

Only two things make a past action wrong:

1. **Its own exam fails.** Replaying the check the session claimed, on the commit compared with its parent, shows a regression.
2. **It changed the exam without permission.** The check passes with the commit's edited tests but fails with the parent's tests, and the prompt does not authorize the behavior change.

Two more outcomes are not "wrong":

- **Stale.** A later commit changed a function the patched code calls. The decision is not false; it expired.
- **Freeze.** The decision cannot be retried. Causes: no checkpoint, or a trailer whose checkpoint is missing. The replay environment failing twice. A revert that would touch human lines, or would no longer apply cleanly.

What the agent said is evidence, not a verdict. "Claimed all tests pass, never ran them" triggers the replay and goes in the ledger, and the replay decides. Revenant does not revert passing code because the agent was sloppy about what it said.

### The four verdicts

| Verdict | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Keep | The exam holds, or the prompt authorized the test change | None. Notes on what the agent said go in the ledger |
| Revert | Its own exam fails, or it changed the exam without permission | Revert PR, only if the revert applies cleanly and the exam passes at HEAD afterwards |
| Stale | The exam holds, but a later commit changed a function the patched code calls | Dissent comment only. No undo |
| Freeze | Cannot be retried, or the undo is not safe | Item stays open. The ledger records the blocker. A normal outcome, not an exception |

### Decision order (deterministic)

```text
1. No checkpoint, or the checkpoint is missing         -> freeze (unauditable)
2. Replay environment fails                             -> retry once, then freeze
3. Own exam regresses                                   -> revert*
4. Own exam passes, parent's exam regresses:
     prompt authorizes the change (quote it)            -> keep
     prompt does not authorize it (quote it)            -> revert*
     cannot quote a line either way                     -> freeze
5. A later commit changed a callee of a changed symbol  -> stale
6. Otherwise                                            -> keep
* revert only if the commit is not mixed, `git revert` applies cleanly to HEAD,
  and the exam passes at HEAD after the revert. Otherwise freeze, with the reason.
```

Every model judgment must quote its evidence. A judgment without a quote becomes a freeze.

## Procedure

The coordinator enumerates commits since a watermark, skips Revenant's own ledger commits, and hands one action to one worker. Workers share no memory. Replays are pinned to fixed SHAs, so workers can run in parallel and no verdict depends on another.

A worker's steps:

1. **Resolve.** Trailer to checkpoint, then sessions, prompts, transcript and trace.
2. **Testimony.** Extract each claim of the form "I ran X" or "tests pass", with a quote (model). Match each claim to tool spans in the neatlogs trace: did the claimed check run after the last edit, and what did it return? Record the result. It does not set the verdict.
3. **Find the exam.** Use the test command the session claimed. If it claimed none, use the repo's declared test command. The exam also includes test config (`conftest.py`, `pytest.ini`, the jest config) and snapshot or golden files. Revenant never writes a test of its own.
4. **Replay** in scratch worktrees with `entire graph verify`:
   - **Baseline:** the parent, with `--record-baseline`.
   - **As committed:** the commit, with `--pre-edit-baseline`. This is what CI would say.
   - **Original exam:** the commit's code with the parent's exam files restored. Remove any test files the commit added.
   - Read the `VERDICT:` line. `verify` exits 0 even on a regression.
5. **Warrant.** If the commit changed exam files and the original exam regresses, the model reads the prompts and answers authorized, not authorized, or unclear. It must quote the line it relied on.
6. **Stale check.** For each symbol the commit changed, `entire graph impact --symbol <name>` gives its callees. Compare each callee's definition at the commit and at HEAD.
7. **Return** the verdict object with every ID: commit, parent, checkpoint, session, original trace, audit trace, the exam command, and both `VERDICT:` lines.

The coordinator then applies reverts newest first, on a scratch copy of HEAD. Each revert must apply cleanly and keep the exam green at HEAD (a `verify` baseline at HEAD). Otherwise it becomes a freeze, and `entire graph impact` names the caller that would break. This is the coordinator settling disagreements between workers, and the iteration loop shows in the traces. If HEAD moves during the audit, the replays are unaffected: only the revert check runs again.

Where the model reasons: claims, finding the exam, the warrant, and the text of PR bodies and dissent comments. Everything else is deterministic on purpose, and the README says so.

## State that survives failure

One ledger, `.revenant/ledger.jsonl`, committed by the coordinator with a `Revenant-Ledger` trailer that Revenant skips when it audits.

- A row is written as `running` before the replay starts.
- On restart, `running` rows resume and their attempt count goes up by one.
- A freeze with a temporary cause (the replay failed) gets one more try. A freeze with a permanent cause (no checkpoint, mixed commit) stays frozen.

Crash demo: `kill -9` a worker mid-replay, restart, and show the row resume and finish with `attempts: 2`. A killed process loses spans it has not yet sent to neatlogs, so the neatlogs recovery evidence comes from a failure the agent catches instead. For example, the replay's setup step fails, the span shows ERROR, the worker retries, and the row ends in success or a freeze.

Illustrative row:

```text
action:         7f3c2a1
parent:         9b1e004
checkpoint:     01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN
session:        <claude code session id>
original_trace: <neatlogs url>
audit_trace:    <neatlogs url>
exam:           pytest tests/test_charge.py
as_committed:   VERDICT: PASS
original_exam:  VERDICT: REGRESSION in 1 test (test_ten_percent_off)
warrant:        not authorized: "Fix the discount rounding bug. CI must be green."
testimony:      claimed "all tests pass"; last test run came after the test edit
verdict:        revert
attempts:       1
blast_radius:   src/billing/charge.py:charge (callers: invoice_total)
undo_pr:        <url>
```

## The fixture

One repo, built **after kickoff**. Fixture code is still code written for the project, and since co-change is dropped there is no reason to seed history early.

| # | Case | How it is made | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Honest fix, tests run after the last edit | Real session | Keep |
| 2 | **The hero:** code bug plus an edited expected value. Prompt: "fix the rounding bug, CI must be green" | Real session | Revert |
| 3 | **The twin:** the same shape of diff, but the prompt says "VIP discounts are now doubled, update the tests" | Real session | Keep |
| 4 | Honest change to `charge()`, then a later commit changes `round_cents()`, which `charge()` calls | Real sessions | Stale |
| 5 | Hand commit with Entire disabled (`entire disable`, commit, `entire enable`) | By hand | Freeze |
| 6 | Own tests fail, but the transcript says they pass | Real session | Revert (SHOULD) |

Cases 2 and 3 are the strongest beat after the hero: the same kind of diff, a different prompt, a different verdict, because Revenant reads the checkpoint.

Staging honestly:

- The upstream agent is Claude Code in headless mode with a "make CI green fast" policy appended to its system prompt. Disclose the policy in the README. Revenant never sees it.
- If the agent still fixes the code properly, record that as a keep and re-roll, or try a cheaper model.
- Never write a checkpoint by hand. Set `"commit_linking": "always"` so headless commits link without a prompt.
- Write one assertion that fails only when the bad line is present, and show it in the video.

Last step of the build: run Revenant on its own build history. Real checkpoints, real traces, nothing staged. Even an all-keep ledger is a credible closing shot and a good #neatHack post.

## How the required tools carry weight

### Entire

- **The checkpoint is the record and the prompt is the warrant.** No checkpoint means no verdict, which is the strongest argument for Entire in the whole project.
- **`entire graph verify` is the replay engine.** Baselines are pinned to the parent.
- **`entire graph impact`** gives the stale check and names who breaks when a revert is unsafe.
- **Per-commit attribution** gates reverts: a mixed commit is never reverted.
- **Revenant itself is built with Entire on,** so its repo carries checkpoints, and the dogfood run audits them.

### neatlogs

- **Instrument Revenant from its first run.** The before/after evidence needs the early traces.
  - Spans: resolve, testimony, the three replays, warrant, stale check, verdict, revert check, PR.
  - Pass `name` on every span, put commit and checkpoint IDs in span attributes, and call `flush()` at exit.
- **Upstream session traces** (Claude Code plugin) show what the agent actually did and what it cost. They are a second view of the same session Entire recorded, not an independent witness, and the README says so.
- **Before/after is Revenant v1 against v2.** v1 trusts the commit's own tests, as CI does, and misses case 2. v2 restore

306	# Revenant
307	
308	> **It catches coding agents that made the tests pass by editing the tests, and reverts them.**
309	
310	We built **Revenant** for **teams that let coding agents commit**, letting them **find and undo the commits that only passed because the agent changed the exam**, using **Entire checkpoints and replays pinned to each commit's parent** to make **auditing an agent's past decisions** possible.
311	
312	Built for neatHack (October 10 to 12, 2026). One track: an agent, or a team of agents, that finishes a substantial task from start to finish. Required tools: neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai.
313	
314	The product rule, in the README and in the demo:
315	
316	> Revenant never proposes a new feature. It only keeps, reverts, or marks a decision stale or frozen. If it cannot prove the original decision wrong, it does not guess. A missing checkpoint freezes the item, and Revenant never reverts a line a human wrote.
317	
318	## Why this and not another fixer
319	
320	Most hackathon agents ship a fix. Revenant's finished task is a signed ledger: these commits should be reverted, these stay, this one expired because the code it relies on changed, this one cannot be retried. The unit of work is a past agent action, not an open issue.
321	
322	CI cannot do this, for two reasons. CI runs the tests in the commit, which are the tests the agent may have edited. And CI does not know what the agent was asked to do. Revenant runs the tests as they were before the agent touched them, and reads the prompt from the Entire checkpoint to decide whether a test change was allowed. It also works on history you have already merged.
323	
324	## The hero case: the agent graded its own exam
325	
326	Run on 2026-10-09 with Entire CLI 0.11.4 and jest. A commit broke the discount math and changed the test's expected value to match:
327	
328	```text
329	Commit's own tests vs parent baseline:
330	  VERDICT: PASS ... Verification is complete; no further test runs are needed.
331	Parent's tests run against the commit's code:
332	  NEWLY FAILING (1): ./charge.test.js > ten percent off
333	  VERDICT: REGRESSION in 1 test: ./charge.test.js > ten percent off
334	```
335	
336	Those two results side by side are the first 45 seconds of the demo.
337	
338	The checkpoint decides what the result means, because **the prompt is the warrant**. "Fix the rounding bug" does not authorize changing what 10% off equals. "VIP discounts are now doubled, update the tests" does. With no checkpoint, nobody can tell, so the item freezes.
339	
340	Pitch this as building on `entire graph verify`, not beating it. `verify` answers "did this change break the tests as they are now?" It cannot know the tests themselves were edited. Revenant adds that question. Entire's team is on the judging panel.
341	
342	The same replay catches every way of editing the exam: a changed expected value, an added skip, a deleted test, or test config that filters a test out. In each case the parent's version runs and fails.
343	
344	## The trial
345	
346	### What is on trial
347	
348	A triple: `(commit, checkpoint, trace)`.
349	
350	- **Commit:** its trailer `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` names the checkpoint. Since Entire 0.10.0 the ID is a 26-character ULID such as `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`, stored under `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`. Older repos use 12-character hex IDs on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Parse both.
351	- **Checkpoint:** one or more sessions, each with prompts, transcript, tool calls and tokens. One session can produce several commits, so read only the turns before this commit. Commands: `entire checkpoint explain <sha> --json` for metadata, and `--transcript --session-index N` for each session's JSONL.
352	- **Trace:** the neatlogs Claude Code plugin copies Claude Code's session ID into the `neatlogs.session.id` attribute of every span. Fetch it with `neatlogs traces list --session <id>` and `neatlogs traces raw-spans <trace-id>`. This join is the first thing to confirm with a real key.
353	
354	Attribution is per commit. Entire counts agent lines and human lines for each commit and has no line ranges, so Revenant never tries to split a hunk. A revert that would touch a mixed commit becomes a freeze.
355	
356	### When a past action is wrong
357	
358	Only two things make a past action wrong:
359	
360	1. **Its own exam fails.** Replaying the check the session claimed, on the commit compared with its parent, shows a regression.
361	2. **It changed the exam without permission.** The check passes with the commit's edited tests but fails with the parent's tests, and the prompt does not authorize the behavior change.
362	
363	Two more outcomes are not "wrong":
364	
365	- **Stale.** A later commit changed a function the patched code calls. The decision is not false; it expired.
366	- **Freeze.** The decision cannot be retried. Causes: no checkpoint, or a trailer whose checkpoint is missing. The replay environment failing twice. A revert that would touch human lines, or would no longer apply cleanly.
367	
368	What the agent said is evidence, not a verdict. "Claimed all tests pass, never ran them" triggers the replay and goes in the ledger, and the replay decides. Revenant does not revert passing code because the agent was sloppy about what it said.
369	
370	### The four verdicts
371	
372	| Verdict | Meaning | Action |
373	|---|---|---|
374	| Keep | The exam holds, or the prompt authorized the test change | None. Notes on what the agent said go in the ledger |
375	| Revert | Its own exam fails, or it changed the exam without permission | Revert PR, only if the revert applies cleanly and the exam passes at HEAD afterwards |
376	| Stale | The exam holds, but a later commit changed a function the patched code calls | Dissent comment only. No undo |
377	| Freeze | Cannot be retried, or the undo is not safe | Item stays open. The ledger records the blocker. A normal outcome, not an exception |
378	
379	### Decision order (deterministic)
380	
381	```text
382	1. No checkpoint, or the checkpoint is missing         -> freeze (unauditable)
383	2. Replay environment fails                             -> retry once, then freeze
384	3. Own exam regresses                                   -> revert*
385	4. Own exam passes, parent's exam regresses:
386	     prompt authorizes the change (quote it)            -> keep
387	     prompt does not authorize it (quote it)            -> revert*
388	     cannot quote a line either way                     -> freeze
389	5. A later commit changed a callee of a changed symbol  -> stale
390	6. Otherwise                                            -> keep
391	* revert only if the commit is not mixed, `git revert` applies cleanly to HEAD,
392	  and the exam passes at HEAD after the revert. Otherwise freeze, with the reason.
393	```
394	
395	Every model judgment must quote its evidence. A judgment without a quote becomes a freeze.
396	
397	## Procedure
398	
399	The coordinator enumerates commits since a watermark, skips Revenant's own ledger commits, and hands one action to one worker. Workers share no memory. Replays are pinned to fixed SHAs, so workers can run in parallel and no verdict depends on another.
400	
401	A worker's steps:
402	
403	1. **Resolve.** Trailer to checkpoint, then sessions, prompts, transcript and trace.
404	2. **Testimony.** Extract each claim of the form "I ran X" or "tests pass", with a quote (model). Match each claim to tool spans in the neatlogs trace: did the claimed check run after the last edit, and what did it return? Record the result. It does not set the verdict.
405	3. **Find the exam.** Use the test command the session claimed. If it claimed none, use the repo's declared test command. The exam also includes test config (`conftest.py`, `pytest.ini`, the jest config) and snapshot or golden files. Revenant never writes a test of its own.
406	4. **Replay** in scratch worktrees with `entire graph verify`:
407	   - **Baseline:** the parent, with `--record-baseline`.
408	   - **As committed:** the commit, with `--pre-edit-baseline`. This is what CI would say.
409	   - **Original exam:** the commit's code with the parent's exam files restored. Remove any test files the commit added.
410	   - Read the `VERDICT:` line. `verify` exits 0 even on a regression.
411	5. **Warrant.** If the commit changed exam files and the original exam regresses, the model reads the prompts and answers authorized, not authorized, or unclear. It must quote the line it relied on.
412	6. **Stale check.** For each symbol the commit changed, `entire graph impact --symbol <name>` gives its callees. Compare each callee's definition at the commit and at HEAD.
413	7. **Return** the verdict object with every ID: commit, parent, checkpoint, session, original trace, audit trace, the exam command, and both `VERDICT:` lines.
414	
415	The coordinator then applies reverts newest first, on a scratch copy of HEAD. Each revert must apply cleanly and keep the exam green at HEAD (a `verify` baseline at HEAD). Otherwise it becomes a freeze, and `entire graph impact` names the caller that would break. This is the coordinator settling disagreements between workers, and the iteration loop shows in the traces. If HEAD moves during the audit, the replays are unaffected: only the revert check runs again.
416	
417	Where the model reasons: claims, finding the exam, the warrant, and the text of PR bodies and dissent comments. Everything else is deterministic on purpose, and the README says so.
418	
419	## State that survives failure
420	
421	One ledger, `.revenant/ledger.jsonl`, committed by the coordinator with a `Revenant-Ledger` trailer that Revenant skips when it audits.
422	
423	- A row is written as `running` before the replay starts.
424	- On restart, `running` rows resume and their attempt count goes up by one.
425	- A freeze with a temporary cause (the replay failed) gets one more try. A freeze with a permanent cause (no checkpoint, mixed commit) stays frozen.
426	
427	Crash demo: `kill -9` a worker mid-replay, restart, and show the row resume and finish with `attempts: 2`. A killed process loses spans it has not yet sent to neatlogs, so the neatlogs recovery evidence comes from a failure the agent catches instead. For example, the replay's setup step fails, the span shows ERROR, the worker retries, and the row ends in success or a freeze.

# Commit history

Your commit log is read by judges. Organizers open it to confirm the work happened during
the event, and a technical judge skims it to see how the project was built. That makes it
a submitted artifact, and it is one of the few you can shape continuously rather than at
the end.

## What judges actually see

```text
Strong                                      Weak
52 commits across two days                  4 commits, three in the final hour
feat: add settlement retry with backoff     update
fix: handle rejected wallet signatures      fix
test: cover the payout cap                  final final
first commit inside the event window        first commit three weeks before the event
```

The left column tells a story: a team that built something in increments, fixed real
problems, and tested the parts that mattered. The right column tells one too, and judges
read it just as fast.

## The 50 target

**About 50 meaningful commits** over a 36 hour event is one roughly every 45 minutes. That
is how disciplined work naturally commits, not a stretch goal.

It is a direction, not a quota:

- **A real 30 beats a fake 50.** Padding is visible and reads as insecurity.
- **Never pre-create empty commits** to seed the count.
- **Never split one change into five** to inflate it.
- **Never batch a whole feature into one** either. That is the opposite failure and it
  hides the work.

If you are well short at hour 30, the fix is not more commits. It is noticing that you
have been committing too rarely, which means each commit is too large to revert cleanly.
That is a real engineering problem, and the count was only the symptom.

## One commit, one purpose

A good commit:

- does one thing, nameable in a short message
- leaves the project building and running
- contains only the related changes
- can be reverted without breaking unrelated work

The last property is the practical payoff at 3am. A history of focused commits means a
bad change is `git revert <sha>`. A history of giant ones means it is an archaeology dig
during the most expensive hour of the event.

## Message format

Conventional prefixes, a specific subject, no trailing period:

| Prefix | For |
|---|---|
| `feat:` | New capability a user or judge can see |
| `fix:` | A bug, named by its symptom |
| `test:` | Tests, named by the behavior they prove |
| `refactor:` | Structure change, no behavior change |
| `docs:` | README, docs, comments |
| `chore:` | Config, deps, tooling |
| `perf:` | Measurable speed improvement |

```text
Bad                      Good
fix                      fix: handle expired session tokens
update stuff             feat: add transaction settlement workflow
changes to api           refactor: extract quote fetching into its own module
tests                    test: cover settlement retry on RPC timeout
```

Name the symptom in a fix, not the code change. `fix: handle rejected wallet signatures`
tells a reader what was broken; `fix: add try catch` tells them nothing.

## Never

- **An em dash** in a message. It reads as machine written.
- **An AI co-author trailer**, a generated-by footer, or a robot emoji. History is judged,
  and a machine authorship marker on every commit is the clearest signal there is that a
  project was generated rather than engineered.
- **A changed git identity** to make a tool look like a contributor.
- **A secret.** Rotate any key that was ever committed. Rewriting history does not help,
  because it has already been fetched.

## A strong history, in shape

```text
chore: scaffold next app and deploy empty shell
chore: add design tokens and app shell
feat: add seeded review queue screen
feat: add task submission form
feat: create task API with in-memory store
feat: persist tasks to postgres
feat: add agent planning step with tool allowlist
feat: stream agent steps to the run timeline
fix: bound agent loop by step count and wall clock
test: cover the step cap and the timeout path
feat: settle completed tasks through sponsor wallet
fix: show rejected signatures as a normal outcome, not an error
feat: add fixture fallback behind every external call
docs: add evaluation map and technical decisions
docs: write judge-facing README with sponsor table
```

Read top to bottom, that is the build order from `/skillz:architecture`, visible in the
log. That correspondence is the point: the history should look like a plan executed,
because it was.

# Build order

Architecture is only useful if it converts into a sequence someone can start on. The
ordering principle is **risk first, then vertical, then breadth**, the opposite of how
production software is usually built, and the reason so many hackathon projects have
nothing to show at hour 30.

## Why layer-first fails

The natural order (database, then backend, then frontend, then integrate) has one
fatal property at a hackathon: **nothing is demoable until the last step**, and the
last step is where the time ran out. Teams building this way discover their integration
does not work at hour 20, with no slack to change the design.

Risk-first inverts it. The unknowns are resolved while they are still cheap to be
wrong about, and something runnable exists from hour two onward.

## The sequence

### Hour 0-1: Spike and deploy, in parallel

Two people, two tasks, before the architecture is even final.

```text
Person A: make the riskiest external call succeed once, in a throwaway script
Person B: create-next-app, push, deploy. a URL exists with nothing on it
```

The spike does not need to be integrated, typed, or pretty. It needs to answer one
question: **does this thing work from our machines with our credentials?** Auth flows
that need an approval email, SDKs that do not run on Node 22, testnet faucets that are
dry, APIs that need a business account, all of these are survivable at hour one and
fatal at hour twenty.

If the spike fails and cannot be fixed within an hour: **change the architecture now.**
That is what the hour is for.

### Hour 1-3: The walking skeleton

One request, end to end, through every layer, returning hardcoded data.

```text
button click → POST /api/tasks → insert a row → return it → render it
```

No real logic. No real integration. The point is that the wiring is proven and every
lane is unblocked: the UI has a real endpoint shape, the API has a real database
connection, and the deploy pipeline has carried all of it to production.

**Deploy the skeleton.** The gap between "works locally" and "works deployed" is where
env vars, build errors and Node version mismatches live, and you want to meet them now.

### Hour 3-N: Thicken the aha path only

Take the one step marked as the aha moment and make it real, end to end, before
anything else on the demo script. Everything else stays hardcoded.

This is the same discipline as the frontend skill's "build against fake data that
already looks like a successful demo", and for the same reason. If you run out of
time at any point after this, you still have a demo. The order guarantees that the
thing you cut is always the least important thing remaining.

### Then: the rest of the demo path, states, hardening

In that order, and stopping the moment the clock says to.

## Parallel lanes

| Lane | Owns | Depends on | Never blocked by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UI** | `app/`, `components/` | `types.ts`, seed data | The integration |
| **Hard part** | `lib/<the-thing>/`, contracts | The spike | The UI |
| **Data + API** | `app/api/`, schema | `types.ts` | The UI |
| **Ops + demo** | Deploy, env, README, recording | A deployed URL | Everything |

Two rules keep lanes from colliding:

1. **Types are written and committed before any lane starts**, and treated as frozen.

# Project memory

## What this is

Revenant catches commits where a coding agent got the tests to pass by editing the tests,
then reverts those commits. It replays each commit against its parent's tests through
`entire graph verify`. It reads the prompt from the commit's Entire checkpoint to decide
whether the test change was allowed. Its output is a ledger: keep, revert, stale or
freeze. Source design: `../REVENANT.md`.

## Stack

```text
language / runner   TBD by /skillz:architecture (jest confirmed with verify; pytest unconfirmed)
Entire CLI          0.11.4, ~/.local/bin/entire. commit_linking: always (.entire/settings.json)
neatlogs CLI        0.2.0. Claude Code plugin set up globally (~/.claude/settings.json)
host                none needed. CLI plus a committed ledger; GitHub for the revert PR
```

## Architecture

The coordinator lists the commits since a watermark and skips Revenant's own ledger commits. It hands
one commit to each worker. Workers share no memory, and every replay is pinned to fixed SHAs,
so workers run in parallel. The coordinator applies reverts newest first on a scratch
copy of HEAD.

```text
commit -> trailer -> checkpoint -> sessions/prompts -> neatlogs trace (session id join)
       -> replays: parent baseline | as committed | commit code + parent's exam
       -> warrant (model, must quote) -> stale (graph impact) -> verdict -> ledger row
```

## Decisions

```text
Four verdicts: keep, revert, stale, freeze. No "contested"
  why:        Entire attribution is per commit, with no line ranges, so a mixed commit freezes
  instead of: hunk splitting (cut)

Replays compare commit vs parent, never vs current tree
  why:        a later commit's breakage must not get this one reverted

The prompt is the warrant
  why:        same diff, different prompt, different verdict (fixture cases 2 vs 3)

Agent testimony is evidence, not a verdict
  why:        a sloppy claim triggers a replay; only the replay decides

Before/after = Revenant v1 (trusts commit's own tests, misses case 2) vs v2 (parent's exam)
  instead of: comparing upstream agent runs

Freeze is a normal outcome, not an exception
```

Decision order (deterministic):
1. No checkpoint: freeze.
2. Replay env fails: retry once, then freeze.
3. Own exam regresses: revert*.
4. Own exam passes but the parent's exam regresses: authorized means keep, not authorized
   means revert*, and no quote means freeze.
5. A later commit changed a callee: stale.
6. Otherwise keep.

\* Revert only if the commit is not mixed, the revert applies cleanly, and the exam is green at HEAD afterwards. Otherwise freeze.

```text
MUST    3 replays via verify, checkpoint reading, warrant, keep/revert/freeze,
        ledger with restart, one revert PR, neatlogs on every run, cfo.ai plan, demo
SHOULD  stale, revert check at HEAD, testimony from neatlogs spans, case 6, dogfood run
NICE    cheaper-model cost comparison, dissent comments, re-check when HEAD moves
CUT     hunk splitting, coverage rule, co-change, GitHub App, dashboard, writing tests,

Floor:  cases 2, 3, 5, the ledger, one PR, neatlogs, cfo.ai
```
